I found the quoted words on the page, word for word, and the candidate passes all four parts of the admission rule. It is not one of his recorded claims.

**1. The page.** The page opened. It is Sutskever's own signed essay in The Batch's New Year issue, published 30 December 2020. It closes with "Ilya Sutskever is a co-founder of OpenAI, where he is chief scientist." The quoted sentence is there exactly: "In 2021, language models will start to become aware of the visual world." The next sentences read: "The next generation of models will be capable of editing and generating images in response to text input, and hopefully they'll understand text better because of the many images they've seen." Because this is his own essay, it counts as a primary source, not news coverage.

**2. The rule.**
- **Part 1 (role):** passes. He was OpenAI's co-founder and chief scientist in December 2020 (that role ran 2015–2024), and the essay speaks for OpenAI ("At OpenAI, we've developed…").
- **Part 2 (forward-looking, about AI):** passes. It says what AI models will do. "Start to become aware of the visual world" is loose on its own. But the essay itself gives a testable reading: models that edit and generate images from text input. This is not a hypothetical.
- **Part 3 (date):** passes. It names 2021, so it would be judged at 31 December 2021.
- **Part 4 (primary source):** passes, as his own words.

**Recorded?** No. His five recorded claim files run from 2023 to 2025, and none is about language models handling images in 2021.

Two other lines in the essay could be checked separately. Neither is part of this candidate:
- "The best models of 2021 will make the best models of 2020 look dull and simple-minded by comparison." This has a date, but the bar is a judgement call.
- "I'm hopeful that we'll see something like it in 2021." This is hedged as "an aspiration," so it is probably out.
